### page_1
Geophys. J. Int.(1999) 137, 691–712
Early Proterozoic palaeomagnetism: new results from the intrusives
and related rocks of the Karelian, Belomorian and Kola provinces,
eastern Fennoscandian Shield
M. A. Fedotova,1 A. N. Khramov,2 B. N. Pisakin1 and A. A. Priyatkin1
1St Petersburg University, Geological Department, University Embankment7/9, St Petersburg,199164, Russia
2All-Russian Petroleum Research and Geological Exploration Institute (VNIGRI), L iteiny39, St. Petersburg,191104, Russia.
E-mail: khram@oloy.spb.su
Accepted 1998 December 17. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22
SUMMARY
The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are
too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic
horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained
new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement
country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian
Shield.
A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated,
and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity
within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12
poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability
criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might
be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are
poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S, 304.8° E, A95=8.3° ; U–Pb age of
2436± 25 Ma), the Voche-Lambina ultramaﬁcs and amphibolites (12.9 ° N, 314.1° E,
A95=8.6° ; Rb–Sr age of 2198 ± 172 Ma), and the Kolvitsa peridotites and schists
(44.2° N, 232.6° E, A95=5.4° ; assigned magnetization age of 1900 Ma). For the Karelian
Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S,
262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S,
308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro-
dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some
NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic
poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic
apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian
APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our
results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support
the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within the Fennoscandian
Shield since Jatulian times (2300–2100 Ma). To help constrain the relative positions of
the various tectonic blocks of the eastern Fennoscandian Shield during pre-Jatulian
times, more new palaeomagnetic and radiometric data need to be added to the available
palaeomagnetic database.
Key words: APW (apparent polar wander), Early Proterozoic, Fennoscandian Shield,
palaeomagnetism.

extent of the relative horizontal movements of the various
lithospheric blocks that make up the Precambrian cratons, the
time of their origin and mode of their consolidation (Gaal &
Gorbatschev 1987) is of special importance in understanding
the nature and style of plate tectonics in the Precambrian.
Palaeomagnetic data oVer the possibility of addressing some of
these questions; until now, however, only the Canadian Shield
has yielded enough Precambrian palaeomagnetic data to indi-
cate signiﬁcant intracratonic movements (Symons 1991). As
for the Fennoscandian Shield, there is as yet no palaeomagnetic
evidence that can resolve that degree of movement.
An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian
Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval
2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained
tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993).
There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that
signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev
& Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the
possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma.
The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional
orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the
formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987).
On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic
palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were
predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian
provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the
Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for
the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction
of the Fennoscandian APWP. Furthermore, the database used Figure 1. Early Proterozoic palaeomagnetism 693
We focus here on those new data which have radiometric
control, ﬁeld tests and rock-magnetic results. Other new data,
which we have recently published (Khramov et al. 1997) and
updated, will be presented in a later section in summary form.
The Monchegorsk ultramaﬁc layered pluton is situated in
the central part of the Kola Peninsula, to the north of the
Pechenga–Varzuga Tectonic Zone (Fig. 1). It is made up of
two limbs (Fig. 2). The northwestern limb consists mainly
of ultramaﬁc rocks (dunites, harzburgites and pyroxenites),
whereas the eastern limb exposes maﬁc-ultramaﬁc rocks of the
upper part of the intrusion (Balashov et al . 1993). Zircons
separated from gabbro-norites of this limb yield a U–Pb age
of 2493± 7M a( 2s errors are quoted in all cases). The pluton
is cut by picritic dykes, which are, in turn, cut by two
generations of metadoleritic dykes. The ages of these dykes
are still being debated, but are probably within the range
2200–1800 Ma (Gorbunovet al. 1985).
The gabbro-doleritic Main Range massif extends south-
wards from the Monchegorsk pluton. These Main Range rocks
have yielded a U–Pb zircon isochron age of 2436 ± 25 Ma
(Bogdanova & Bibikova 1993). Palaeomagnetic sampling was
carried out in all the structures mentioned above (Fig. 2).
The Voche–Lambina area is located west of Lake Imandra,
along the line of the Pechenga–Varzuga Tectonic Zone (Fig. 1).
The area has been described as the contact zone between
‘Saamian’ orthogneisses and Lopian supracrustal rocks
representing a greenstone belt (Dalyet al. 1993). Lopian rocks
form a sequence of metamorphosed acid, intermediate and
maﬁc volcanics, and clastic sediments that tectonically overlie
‘Saamian’ gneisses. The supracrustals have been divided into
four ‘formations’; however, all of the contacts between these are
interpreted as tectonic (Fig. 2). The metamorphic rocks exhibit
an amphibolite facies alteration (approximately 610–620 ° C),
but locally the rocks have experienced younger epidote-
amphibolite facies metamorphism (430–520° C). The youngest
doleritic dykes, which cut all these rocks, show a faint auto-
metamorphism. These dykes are mostly of Svecofennian
(1880–1810 Ma) age (Gorbunovet al. 1985). Many of the ages
for metamorphic rocks have been interpreted as secondary,
especially Rb–Sr isochrons. These data have been summarized
by Mitrofanov et al. (1991), with the oldest gneisses yielding
a Rb–Sr age of 2540 ± 46 Ma. These gneisses are cut by
granodiorites which gave a Rb–Sr age of 2198± 172 Ma. The
underlying ‘Saamian’ gneisses yielded a U–Pb zircon age of
2801± 9 Ma, indicating a Late Archaean (Lopian) age for
these gneisses. A Lopian rhyodacite from formation IV (Fig. 2)

Formation and the overlying red quartzites of the Shoksha
Formation; near the formation margin, two basaltic ﬂows were
observed. The strata are intruded by the Ropruchey Sill. This
layered lopolith-like sill is some 170 m thick and covers an
area of about 4500 km 2. The outcrops of the sill form two
wings: the western outcrops in the Ladva area consist mainly
of gabbro and gabbroic syenites from the central layers of
the sill, whereas the eastern outcrops in the Shoksha and
Sheltozero areas are made up of dolerites from the bottom
part of the sill. These dolerites are cut by monzonite veins,
related to the last stage of sill emplacement. Similar veins are
also observed in the quartzites of the Shoksha Formation.
In the Rybreka area (not sampled here) located near the
Sheltozero area, zircons from the monzonites yield a U–Pb
age of 1770± 12 Ma (Bibikova et al. 1990). The U–Pb age of
the authigenic minerals from the Petrozavodsk Formation is
1810± 100 Ma, while the K–Ar age of the Ropruchey Sill
is 1690–1640 Ma (Semikhatov 1974). Samples from this sill
were taken in the Sheltozero, Shoksha and Ladva areas (Fig. 3).
The Burakovka maﬁc-ultramaﬁc intrusion, which cuts the
Archean and Lower Proterozoic gneisses and granites, was
examined in the eastern Trans-Onega region (Fig. 3). The
intrusion covers an area of about 800 km 2 and is associated
with a deep fault. The massif consists of three blocks: the
Burakovka, Central and Aganozero blocks. Its cross-sectional Figure 4. Geological sketch map of the Ignoila palaeovolcano,

4.2.6 Burakovka area
Ultramaﬁtes are found amongst the samples from the Aganozero
block of the Burakovka layered intrusion. Thermomagnetic
analysis of these samples gives results that are characteristic
for magnesium magnetite with a small percentage of MgO,
which indicates a primary origin for this magnetite. On the
other hand, petrographic and microprobe investigations
have established the presence of secondary olivine-generated
magnetite, which appeared during serpentinization of the
Aganozero peridotites (Pisakin et al. 1992). Thermomagnetic
analysis of gabbro-norites yields Jrs(T ) dependences charac-
teristic of virtually pure magnetite, whereas the decay curves
Jn(T ) (see Fig. 8, sample B59), in conjunction with microscopic
and microprobe analyses, indicate a thermoremanent origin
of the NRM in the gabbro-norites. These latter rocks, which
contain so-called ‘cloudy’ plagioclase, yield results that are
consistent with the formation of magnetite within such plagio-
clase during the consolidation of the Burakovka intrusion
(Pisakin et al. 1992).
To summarize, the thermomagnetic and (less extensive)
microprobe analyses indicate that many of the studied maﬁc
and ultramaﬁc rocks of the Karelia–Kola region contain
a ferrimagnetic mineral of the magnetite group, syngenetic
with and synchronous with the formation of these rocks:
magnesium-aluminium-chrome magnetite in most ultramaﬁc
and maﬁc rocks, and titanomagnetite, with appreciable amounts
(a) (b)
(c) (d)
(e) (f)
of magnesium and aluminium, in dolerites. Such a mineralogy
